newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk troops suffer trauma in Kurdish rebel fight.
newsitem.headline: Turk troops suffer trauma in Kurdish rebel fight.

text.p: A confidential military study reveals that the Kurdish guerrilla war in southeast Turkey is causing a wide range of psychological trauma among Turkish troops comparable with the American experience in Vietnam.
Disorders afflicting Turkish soldiers include depression, schizophrenia, loss of memory and insomnia, according to the study by a member of Ankara's Gulhane Military Medical Academy.

"In a fighting environment, waiting without knowing where the danger will come from, helplessness, not trusting your own strength and the probability you will be unable to...cope with the danger are all factors that cause intense physical and psychological complaints," it says.
A copy of the study was obtained by Reuters through the private nationwide UBA news agency. A spokeswoman for the academy confirmed the study existed but refused further comment.
Turkish troops have been fighting for 12 years against separatist guerrillas of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) in the mountainous southeast. More than 21,000 people have died.

Military officials acknowledge conditions are difficult for the army because inexperienced conscripts and the regular army are pitted against hardened guerrillas. The fighting shows little signs of subsiding despite repeated official claims that the rebels are on the brink of defeat.
Weeping families accompanying the bodies of their martyred sons to the grave is still a regular feature on Turkish news.

The report, which consists of a study of troops who have served in the southeast and who have undergone psychiatric treatment, says some have symptoms similar to those suffered by U.S. soldiers during the Vietnam War.

Observers say the Turkish fight is similar to Vietnam, in that inexperienced government troops are forced to fight a prolonged guerrilla war against an unseen enemy. Both sides have been accused of committing abuses against civilians.

"Those who have taken part in the fighting become very sensitive towards criticism and can feel guilty because of what they have had to do to stay alive or because they have survived at all," the study says.
The study does not specify what percentage of soldiers -- many of whom are conscripts in their early 20s -- were affected.

The most common condition was antisocial behaviour, encountered in 27.8 percent of the soldiers in the study. These people have problems controlling their impulses, have a low tolerance threshold and are awkward in social intercourse.
Many of them are aggressive and the undisciplined behaviour adversely affects the morale of other soldiers, the study says.
"Anti-social behaviour has been found in 27 percent of Amerian seamen in Vietnam who reported psychiatric problems during war," the study says.
Turkish newspapers have reported instances of demobilised soldiers killing themselves.

A youth from the southeastern province of Mardin shot himself dead with a hunting rifle two months after completing his military service. He was apparently traumatised after eight of his friends died in fighting the PKK.
His family reported problems as soon as he came back from military service. He often told them: "The PKK will come here and kill you all."
The study says other problems reported include sudden paralysis in the hands or feet, fainting, anxiety, and post- traumatic stress disorder similar to a syndrome seen in Vietnam.
"The life of a soldier, particularly the most basic duty of fighting, is completely full of heavy psychological and physical stress factors," the study says.
